questions.stem: Which is a common reason for law reform?
options: A law has been in force for more than ten years and so must be replaced
A court has applied a law correctly in a case that the losing party disliked
A law was passed by a previous government, so the new government must repeal it
Community values have changed, so an existing law no longer reflects them
questions.explanation: Laws should reflect the values of society, so when those values shift, a law may become outdated and need reform. The age of a law, or which government passed it, is not by itself a reason to change it.

questions.stem: Laws written before smartphones existed did not cover sharing intimate images online without consent, so parliament created new offences. Which reason for law reform is best shown?
options: Changes in technology have created situations that existing laws did not address
Changes in the Constitution have given the states new powers over communications
A High Court decision has declared the earlier laws invalid under section 109
A referendum has required the Victorian Parliament to update its criminal laws
questions.explanation: New technology often creates conduct that older laws did not foresee, so parliament reforms the law to deal with it. No constitutional change or referendum is needed for a state to create a new criminal offence.

questions.stem: Which reason for law reform is shown when a law is changed because it treats one group of people less favourably than others without good reason?
options: To reduce the number of laws passed by parliament
To strengthen the doctrine of binding precedent
To transfer residual powers to the Commonwealth
To protect rights and achieve equality before the law
questions.explanation: Reform is often needed to remove unjustified discrimination so that the law treats people equally and protects their rights. Reducing the number of laws or transferring powers is not the aim of such a reform.

questions.stem: A petition to the Victorian Parliament is:
options: a court action brought by a group of people who are all seeking compensation for a shared loss
a public march organised by a group of people to show their support for a cause
a report of the Victorian Law Reform Commission tabled in parliament by its chair
a formal written request, signed by members of the public, that is tabled in parliament
questions.explanation: A petition is a formal request to parliament, signed by people who support it, and presented (tabled) by a member of parliament. A public march is a demonstration, and a group court action is a class action.

questions.stem: Which is the main strength of a petition as a means of influencing law reform?
options: It creates a binding precedent that courts must follow until parliament acts
It forces a referendum once the petition is signed by more than half of voters
It can show members of parliament how many people support a change to the law
It requires parliament to debate and pass a bill reflecting the petition's request
questions.explanation: A large petition shows the level of community concern about an issue and can raise awareness among members of parliament. Parliament is not obliged to act on a petition, and petitions do not trigger referendums in Australia.

questions.stem: A petition with 40,000 signatures calling for a law change is tabled, but no change follows. Which is the most likely reason a petition alone often fails to bring about reform?
options: Petitions can be tabled only in the Commonwealth Parliament, not in the Victorian Parliament
Petitions must first be approved by the Victorian Law Reform Commission before they can be tabled
Parliament is not bound to act on it, and petitions may attract little media or political attention
Petitions are valid only if they are signed by a majority of the voters in every Victorian electorate
questions.explanation: Petitions are a recognised way to raise an issue, but parliament has no obligation to respond with legislation, and many attract little public attention. Victorian Parliament accepts petitions, including e-petitions, without any approval from the VLRC.

questions.stem: Thousands of people march through Melbourne calling for stronger laws on climate change. Which is the most likely way this demonstration could influence law reform?
options: It can require the Victorian Parliament to hold an urgent vote on each of the demonstrators' demands
It can create a precedent that the courts must apply when deciding climate change cases
It can directly amend the relevant Act if the number of people taking part is large enough
It can attract media coverage that raises awareness and puts pressure on members of parliament
questions.explanation: Demonstrations draw public and media attention to an issue, which can increase pressure on law-makers to act. They have no legal power to force a vote, amend an Act or bind a court.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant weakness of demonstrations as a means of influencing law reform?
options: Demonstrations cannot be reported in the media, so they rarely reach a wide audience at all
Unlawful or violent conduct by some participants can turn public opinion against the cause
Demonstrations can only be held with the written permission of the Victorian Law Reform Commission
Demonstrations automatically lead to criminal charges against everyone who takes part in them
questions.explanation: If a demonstration becomes disruptive or violent, media coverage may focus on that conduct rather than the message, which can reduce support for the reform. Peaceful demonstrations are lawful and widely reported.

questions.stem: How can individuals use the courts to influence law reform?
options: By bringing a case that leads a court to set a new precedent or to declare a law invalid
By asking a judge to draft a new bill and then present it to parliament for a vote on it
By applying to the court for an order requiring parliament to change a statute
By lodging a petition with the court, which then refers the issue to a referendum
questions.explanation: A case can lead a court to develop the common law, interpret a statute in a new way or strike down an invalid law, as in Mabo (No 2) and Roach. Courts cannot draft bills or order parliament to legislate.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest limitation on using the courts to bring about law reform?
options: Cases are expensive and slow, and a person must have standing to bring one
Courts may only change laws that were passed by parliament more than twenty years ago
Courts are not permitted to hear cases on matters of public importance
Courts can only change laws when parliament gives them permission first
questions.explanation: Litigation is costly and can take years, and the requirement for standing means only those directly affected can bring a case. There is no age limit on laws a court can consider, and courts often hear cases of public importance.

questions.stem: Which is a way the media can influence law reform?
options: By deciding cases that set new precedents for the lower courts
By approving bills before they can receive royal assent
By raising public awareness of an issue and putting pressure on law-makers
By drafting legislation and introducing it into parliament for debate
questions.explanation: The media, including social media, can bring an issue to public attention, shape opinion and pressure members of parliament to act. Drafting bills, deciding cases and giving royal assent are roles of parliament, courts and the Crown.

questions.stem: A hashtag campaign about a loophole in the law is shared hundreds of thousands of times within a week. Which is the most likely strength of social media in this situation?
options: It allows users to vote directly on whether the law should change
It can spread a message quickly and cheaply to a very large audience
It ensures that only accurate information is shared about the issue online
It requires the government to respond formally within six weeks
questions.explanation: Social media lets individuals and groups reach large audiences quickly and at little cost, which can build momentum for reform. It does not guarantee accuracy, create any formal obligation on government or give users a vote.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant weakness of social media as a means of influencing law reform?
options: Misinformation can spread quickly, and campaigns may lose attention before any change is made
Social media posts are reviewed by parliament, which slows the progress of every reform
Social media can be used only by registered groups, which excludes individuals from campaigns
Social media campaigns are illegal in Victoria if they call for a change to an existing law
questions.explanation: Inaccurate claims can spread as fast as accurate ones, and online attention often moves on quickly, so a campaign may fade before parliament acts. Anyone can use social media, and calling for a change to the law is lawful.

questions.stem: A newspaper runs a long investigation exposing failures in a government agency, and parliament later changes the relevant law. This best shows that traditional media can influence law reform by:
options: introducing a private member's bill that reflects its findings
compelling witnesses to give evidence about the agency's failures
making recommendations that parliament is legally bound to adopt
investigating issues in depth and keeping them in the public eye
questions.explanation: Investigative journalism can uncover problems and keep public attention on them, building pressure for reform. The media has no power to compel witnesses or introduce bills, and its views do not bind parliament.

questions.stem: The Victorian Law Reform Commission is best described as:
options: a Commonwealth body that reviews whether Victorian laws are consistent with the Constitution
an independent, government-funded body that investigates and recommends changes to Victorian law
a committee of members of parliament that has the power to pass laws without a vote in parliament
a court that hears appeals on questions of law from decisions of the Victorian tribunals
questions.explanation: The VLRC is an independent body, funded by the state government, that investigates areas of law and makes recommendations for reform. It cannot pass laws or decide cases, and it is a Victorian, not a Commonwealth, body.

questions.stem: Who can refer a large law reform inquiry to the Victorian Law Reform Commission?
options: Any member of the Victorian public
The Governor-General of Australia
The Attorney-General of Victoria
The Chief Justice of the High Court
questions.explanation: Major inquiries are referred to the VLRC by the Attorney-General. The VLRC can also start small community law reform projects itself, often after suggestions from the public, but members of the public cannot give it a formal reference.

questions.stem: The Victorian Law Reform Commission begins a project on a minor legal issue of general community concern without a reference. This is known as:
options: a parliamentary committee inquiry
a Royal Commission inquiry
a referral of legislative power
a community law reform project
questions.explanation: The VLRC can initiate community law reform projects on relatively minor legal issues of general community concern without a reference from the Attorney-General. Larger inquiries need a reference.

questions.stem: How does the Victorian Law Reform Commission usually gather information during an inquiry?
options: By asking the High Court to rule on the issues before it publishes its final report to parliament
By publishing consultation papers, receiving submissions and holding consultations with the community and experts
By compelling witnesses to appear at public hearings and questioning them under oath in a courtroom
By holding a referendum so that the people of Victoria can vote on each of its draft recommendations in turn
questions.explanation: The VLRC consults widely: it publishes consultation papers, invites submissions and meets with the community, experts and affected groups. Coercive powers to compel witnesses belong to Royal Commissions, not the VLRC.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the ability of the Victorian Law Reform Commission to influence law reform?
options: Its members are elected by voters, so its recommendations are always adopted, but its inquiries are very expensive
Its independence and wide consultation give its reports credibility, but parliament is not bound to adopt its recommendations
Its power to compel witnesses gives its findings great weight, but it can only investigate matters chosen for it by the High Court
Its recommendations become law automatically after six months, but it can only investigate criminal law matters
questions.explanation: The VLRC's expertise, independence and broad consultation make its recommendations persuasive, and many have been implemented. However, it can only recommend, and parliament decides whether to act. It has no coercive powers and its commissioners are appointed, not elected.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation on the Victorian Law Reform Commission's ability to influence law reform?
options: Its final reports are kept secret and are never tabled in parliament or released to the public
Its inquiries must be completed within one month, so the issues cannot be properly researched
Large inquiries depend on references from the Attorney-General, and the government may not act on its reports
It may only investigate laws that were made by the courts, not any Acts that have been passed by the parliament
questions.explanation: The VLRC relies on the Attorney-General for references on significant issues, and whether its recommendations become law depends on the government and parliament. Its reports are tabled in parliament and published, and it reviews both statute and common law.

questions.stem: In 2005 Victoria abolished the partial defence of provocation, following a recommendation of the Victorian Law Reform Commission in its earlier inquiry into defences to homicide. This best shows that:
options: the VLRC can influence law reform when parliament chooses to implement its recommendations
the VLRC can change the law directly by publishing its final report on a matter
the VLRC can overrule common law defences that are inconsistent with community values
the VLRC can require parliament to adopt every recommendation it makes within a year
questions.explanation: The VLRC recommended abolishing provocation, and parliament then passed legislation to do so, showing its influence depends on parliament acting. The VLRC cannot change or overrule the law itself.

questions.stem: A Royal Commission is:
options: an inquiry set up by the government into a matter of public importance, with powers to compel witnesses
a permanent committee of judges that reviews every bill before it is debated in either House of parliament
a permanent body of members of parliament that investigates matters referred by the parliament
a court that hears criminal cases involving members of the royal family and their staff
questions.explanation: A Royal Commission is a formal public inquiry, established by the Governor or Governor-General on the government's advice, with coercive powers such as compelling witnesses and documents. A body of members of parliament is a parliamentary committee.

questions.stem: Who sets the terms of reference for a Victorian Royal Commission?
options: The government, which establishes the Royal Commission
The Royal Commissioner, once the inquiry is underway
The Victorian Law Reform Commission, at the minister's request
The Supreme Court, after hearing submissions from the parties
questions.explanation: The government decides to establish a Royal Commission and sets its terms of reference, which define what it may investigate. This means the inquiry's scope is controlled by the government of the day.

questions.stem: Which is the main strength of a Royal Commission in influencing law reform?
options: Its recommendations must be implemented by parliament within twelve months
Its inquiries are always completed quickly and at little cost to taxpayers
Its members are elected and so represent the views of the community
Its coercive powers let it uncover evidence that might otherwise remain hidden
questions.explanation: Compelling witnesses and documents allows a Royal Commission to uncover the full extent of a problem, giving its findings great weight. Its recommendations are not binding, and Royal Commissions are often long and expensive.

questions.stem: The Royal Commission into Family Violence (Victoria, 2015–16) made 227 recommendations, and the government committed to implementing all of them. Which statement best evaluates the ability of Royal Commissions to influence law reform?
options: They can prompt major reform when the government accepts their recommendations, but implementation depends on the government
They change the law directly once their final report is tabled, so the government has no role at all in implementing them
They are always ignored by government, because their recommendations are made by unelected commissioners
They can only influence law reform in the criminal justice system, not in areas such as health or social services
questions.explanation: When a government commits to a Royal Commission's recommendations, it can lead to wide-ranging reform, as here. But recommendations have no legal force on their own, so their influence depends on the government and parliament acting.

questions.stem: Which is a significant weakness of Royal Commissions as a means of influencing law reform?
options: They have no power to compel witnesses, so they depend entirely on voluntary written submissions from the public
They can only investigate matters chosen by the Victorian Law Reform Commission and its chair
They must hold all their hearings in private, so the public never learns of the evidence given
They can be very expensive and lengthy, and the government is not obliged to implement their findings
questions.explanation: Royal Commissions often run for years at great cost, and their recommendations need not be adopted. They do have coercive powers and usually hold public hearings.

questions.stem: A parliamentary committee is:
options: a group of senior public servants who prepare the final wording of every bill that is introduced into parliament
a group of members of parliament that investigates matters referred to it and reports back to parliament
a group of judges appointed by parliament to hear appeals on the meaning of the Constitution
a group of community members chosen at random to decide whether bills should be passed
questions.explanation: Parliamentary committees are made up of members of parliament, often from different parties, who investigate issues, take submissions and hold hearings, then report with recommendations to parliament. Drafting bills is the work of parliamentary counsel, not committees.

questions.stem: A Victorian parliamentary committee's inquiry into the handling of child abuse by religious and other organisations led to the removal of the limitation period for civil claims about child abuse. This best shows that:
options: parliamentary committees can change the law themselves without a vote in either House
parliamentary committees can only investigate matters already decided by the High Court
parliamentary committees must have their recommendations approved by referendum
parliamentary committees can influence law reform when their recommendations are acted on
questions.explanation: The Betrayal of Trust inquiry recommended reforms, and parliament later legislated, including removing the limitation period for child abuse claims. Committees only recommend; parliament makes the change.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares parliamentary committees with Royal Commissions as law reform bodies?
options: Committees are always more expensive and lengthy, whereas Royal Commissions report within a few weeks of being established
Committees are set up by the Governor-General, whereas Royal Commissions are set up by a vote of the Legislative Council
Committees are made up of members of parliament close to law-making, whereas Royal Commissions are led by independent commissioners with coercive powers
Committees can compel any witness and pass laws themselves, whereas Royal Commissions can only receive written submissions
questions.explanation: Committee members are themselves law-makers, which can help recommendations progress, but their work may reflect party politics. Royal Commissions are independent and have strong investigative powers, though they are costly and their findings are not binding.

questions.stem: Which is a weakness of parliamentary committees as a means of influencing law reform?
options: Their inquiries can only be started by a referendum, so they are rarely used to investigate issues
Members may be influenced by party politics, and the government is not bound to accept their reports
Members must be former judges, so the committee often lacks community or political experience
Their reports are not tabled in parliament, so other members never learn about their recommendations
questions.explanation: Committee members belong to political parties, so findings may be shaped by party positions, and the government can decline to act on them. Committee reports are tabled in parliament, and members are elected politicians, not judges.

questions.stem: Under section 128 of the Constitution, before a proposed change to the Constitution is put to a referendum, it must generally be:
options: approved by the High Court as consistent with the rest of the existing Constitution
passed by the parliaments of at least four of the six Australian states
signed by the Prime Minister and the premiers of every state and territory
passed by an absolute majority of both Houses of the Commonwealth Parliament
questions.explanation: A proposal to alter the Constitution must first be passed as a bill by an absolute majority of both Houses (or, in limited circumstances, by one House twice). It then goes to the voters; state parliaments and the High Court do not approve it.

questions.stem: A double majority in a referendum means:
options: a national majority of voters and a majority of voters in a majority of states
a majority of voters in both the Senate and the House of Representatives
a majority of voters in two consecutive referendums on the same proposal
a two-thirds majority of voters across Australia and in the territories
questions.explanation: A proposal passes only if a majority of voters nationally and a majority of voters in at least four of the six states approve it. Territory voters count towards the national total but not towards the state majority.

questions.stem: In a referendum, 54% of voters nationally vote Yes, with Yes majorities in New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania only. What is the result?
options: The proposal fails, because it did not win a majority in at least four states
The proposal succeeds, because it won a majority of voters across Australia
The proposal succeeds, because it won in the two states with the most voters
The proposal fails, because it needed a two-thirds majority of voters nationally
questions.explanation: A national majority is not enough: the proposal also needs majorities in at least four of the six states, and it won only three. No two-thirds majority is required.

questions.stem: Which is a reason for constitutional reform?
options: The High Court cannot interpret the Constitution until it has been updated
The states cannot make any laws until the Constitution recognises them again
The Constitution was drafted in the 1890s and may not reflect modern values
The Constitution must be rewritten in full every fifty years under section 128
questions.explanation: The Constitution was written in the 1890s, so some argue it should be updated to reflect today's values, for example by recognising First Nations peoples or protecting more rights. Section 128 sets a process for change but requires no regular rewriting.

questions.stem: Which factor is most strongly associated with the success of a referendum?
options: A Yes campaign run by only one political party
A low level of public awareness about the proposal
Bipartisan support from the major political parties
A long and complex proposal covering many changes
questions.explanation: Referendums are far more likely to succeed when the major parties agree, as in 1967. Complex proposals, partisan campaigns and low public understanding all make a Yes result less likely.

questions.stem: Of the many referendums held since Federation, only eight have succeeded. Which statement best explains this record?
options: Voting at referendums is optional, so very few people vote and proposals rarely reach the required level of support
Referendums can only succeed if every state and territory votes Yes, which has happened on very few occasions
The double majority is hard to achieve, and voters tend to reject proposals they do not fully understand or that lack bipartisan support
Most referendums have been declared invalid by the High Court because they did not follow the process set out in section 128
questions.explanation: The double majority sets a high bar, and voters have often been cautious, voting No when a proposal is unclear or opposed by a major party. Voting is compulsory, and only a majority of states, not all states, is required.

questions.stem: What did the 1967 referendum about First Nations people change?
options: It added a preamble to the Constitution that recognised Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples as first peoples
It allowed the Commonwealth to make special laws for Aboriginal people and allowed them to be counted in the census
It gave Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people the right to vote in Commonwealth elections for the first time
It gave Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people Australian citizenship, which they had not held until then
questions.explanation: The 1967 referendum removed the words in section 51(xxvi) that excluded Aboriginal people from the Commonwealth's race power, and repealed section 127, which had excluded them from population counts. It did not grant voting rights or citizenship, which is a common misconception.

questions.stem: The 1967 referendum was approved by about 91% of voters and carried in all six states. Which factor best explains this result?
options: The proposal had bipartisan support in parliament and wide community support
The proposal was opposed by the government, which made voters more interested
The proposal required only a national majority rather than a double majority
The proposal was put to voters alongside a vote on becoming a republic
questions.explanation: The 1967 proposal was supported by both sides of politics and had strong community backing, which helped it win the highest Yes vote of any Australian referendum. It still needed a double majority, and the republic referendum was not held until 1999.

questions.stem: The 2023 referendum proposed to alter the Constitution to:
options: replace the Crown with an Australian head of state chosen by the Commonwealth Parliament
recognise Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples by establishing a body called the Voice
give Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples the right to vote in all Commonwealth elections
allow the Commonwealth to make special laws for Aboriginal people and count them in the census
questions.explanation: The 2023 proposal would have recognised Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples by establishing the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice, which could make representations to parliament and the executive government. Special laws and the census were the subject of 1967.

questions.stem: What was the outcome of the 2023 referendum about an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice?
options: It was carried nationally, but failed because it won a majority in only three states
It was carried, because it won a majority in four states and the territories
It was not carried, because the High Court ruled the proposal was invalid
It was not carried, failing to win a national majority or a majority in any state
questions.explanation: The proposal was rejected by a majority of voters nationally and in every state, with only the Australian Capital Territory recording a Yes majority. The High Court played no part in the result.

questions.stem: Which factor most clearly contributed to the different results of the 1967 and 2023 referendums?
options: The 1967 proposal was decided by parliament alone, whereas the 2023 proposal was put to the voters to decide
The 1967 proposal had bipartisan support, whereas the 2023 proposal was opposed by the major opposition parties
The 1967 proposal needed only a national majority, whereas the 2023 proposal needed a double majority to succeed
Voting was compulsory in 1967 but optional in 2023, so far fewer people took part in the later referendum
questions.explanation: Bipartisan support is widely seen as key to referendum success: it was present in 1967 but absent in 2023, when the major opposition parties campaigned for No. Both referendums needed a double majority, both were decided by voters, and voting was compulsory in both.
